Two-part models

Source: vignettes/two-part.Rmd
two-part.Rmd

A two-part model is used when an outcome is the product of a mix of two processes, one for observed zeroes and non-zeroes, and one for an amount among the non-zeroes. The expected outcome is the product of the two:

E(y)=Pr⁡(y>0)×E(y∣y>0)E(y) = \Pr(y > 0) \times E(y \mid y > 0)

In R, fit the two parts as separate models and combine them with suest() and the twopart option. Predictions and marginal effects from marginaleffects are then on the expected outcome, with standard errors from the joint covariance of the two parts.

The examples use the medical expenditures of 19,386 adults in the 2004 Medical Expenditure Panel Survey. The first part is a logit of whether a person had any medical expenditures. The second part is a Poisson model of expenditures among the people who had any. With the robust standard errors suest() computes, this is Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood: it fits a model of the mean of any outcome that is zero or positive, not only counts, and needs only the model of the mean to be right (Santos Silva and Tenreyro 2006). family = quasipoisson fits it without warnings about outcomes that are not whole numbers.

Fit the two parts and combine them

Both parts cluster on the dwelling unit (duid):

library(suest)
library(marginaleffects)
library(haven)

meps <- zap_labels(read_dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/meps.dta"))
meps[c("female", "ins_unins", "anylim")] <-
  lapply(meps[c("female", "ins_unins", "anylim")], factor)
table(meps$exp_tot > 0)
#> 
#> FALSE  TRUE 
#>  3440 15946

any <- glm(I(exp_tot > 0) ~ age + female + lninc + pcs12 + mcs12 + ins_unins +
             anylim, family = binomial, data = meps)
amount <- glm(exp_tot ~ age + female + lninc + pcs12 + mcs12 + ins_unins +
                anylim, family = quasipoisson, data = meps, subset = exp_tot > 0)

fit <- suest(any, amount, model_names = c("Any", "Amount"), cluster = "duid",
             twopart = TRUE)
summary(fit)
#> 
#> Simultaneous results for Any, Amount                      Number of obs = 19,386
#>                                         (Std. err. adjusted for 10,940 clusters)
#> 
#> --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#>               |                 Robust
#>               | Coefficient  std. err.        z   P>|z|     [95% conf. interval]
#> --------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------
#> Any           |
#>   (Intercept) |      -0.695      0.342   -2.033   0.042       -1.364      -0.025
#>           age |       0.030      0.002   19.358   0.000        0.027       0.033
#>       female1 |       0.957      0.044   21.744   0.000        0.871       1.044
#>         lninc |       0.349      0.026   13.273   0.000        0.298       0.401
#>         pcs12 |      -0.040      0.003  -12.130   0.000       -0.046      -0.033
#>         mcs12 |      -0.016      0.003   -6.430   0.000       -0.021      -0.011
#>    ins_unins1 |      -1.644      0.050  -32.946   0.000       -1.742      -1.546
#>       anylim1 |       0.799      0.073   10.991   0.000        0.657       0.942
#> --------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------
#> Amount        |
#>   (Intercept) |       9.183      0.284   32.360   0.000        8.627       9.739
#>           age |       0.011      0.001    8.146   0.000        0.008       0.014
#>       female1 |       0.046      0.039    1.180   0.238       -0.031       0.124
#>         lninc |       0.066      0.022    3.034   0.002        0.023       0.109
#>         pcs12 |      -0.036      0.002  -18.391   0.000       -0.040      -0.033
#>         mcs12 |      -0.012      0.002   -6.746   0.000       -0.015      -0.009
#>    ins_unins1 |      -0.910      0.064  -14.169   0.000       -1.036      -0.784
#>       anylim1 |       0.362      0.040    9.146   0.000        0.284       0.439
#> --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

With survey data, put the weights and clusters in a svydesign(), fit the first part to the full design and the second part to the people with any expenditures, and give suest() the full design. wts = TRUE averages with the sampling weights:

design <- survey::svydesign(ids = ~duid, weights = ~wtdper, data = meps)
any_s <- survey::svyglm(I(exp_tot > 0) ~ age + female + lninc + pcs12 + mcs12 +
                          ins_unins + anylim, design = design,
                        family = quasibinomial)
amount_s <- survey::svyglm(exp_tot ~ age + female + lninc + pcs12 + mcs12 +
                             ins_unins + anylim,
                           design = subset(design, exp_tot > 0),
                           family = quasipoisson)
fit_s <- suest(any_s, amount_s, survey_design = design,
               observation_id = "dupersid", twopart = TRUE)
avg_slopes(fit_s, variables = c("age", "ins_unins"), wts = TRUE)
#> 
#>       Term Contrast Estimate Std. Error     z Pr(>|z|)     S   2.5 %  97.5 %
#>  age          dY/dX     55.3       5.42  10.2   <0.001  78.9    44.7    65.9
#>  ins_unins    1 - 0  -2595.1     163.67 -15.9   <0.001 185.7 -2915.9 -2274.3
#> 
#> Type: response

Expected expenditures and effects on them

Predictions are the product of the two parts: the probability of any expenditures from Any times the expected expenditures of someone who has any from Amount:

avg_predictions(fit)
#> 
#>  Estimate Std. Error    z Pr(>|z|)   S 2.5 % 97.5 %
#>      3681         65 56.7   <0.001 Inf  3554   3809
#> 
#> Type: response
avg_slopes(fit, variables = c("age", "female", "ins_unins", "anylim"))
#> 
#>       Term Contrast Estimate Std. Error      z Pr(>|z|)     S   2.5 %  97.5 %
#>  age          dY/dX     48.6       4.96   9.80  < 0.001  72.9    38.9    58.3
#>  anylim       1 - 0   1532.8     151.64  10.11  < 0.001  77.4  1235.6  1830.0
#>  female       1 - 0    416.8     140.81   2.96  0.00308   8.3   140.8   692.7
#>  ins_unins    1 - 0  -2701.0     113.17 -23.87  < 0.001 415.8 -2922.8 -2479.2
#> 
#> Type: response

Expected expenditures average about $3,680 a year. Being uninsured is associated with $2,700 less in expenditure; each year of age predicts a $49 increase; being female, a $417 increase; and having any activity limitation, a $1,533 increase.

Effects in each part

type = "positive" gives the effect on the probability of any expenditures, and type = "amount" the effect on the expected expenditures of someone who has any:

avg_comparisons(fit, variables = "ins_unins", type = "positive")
#> 
#>  Estimate Std. Error     z Pr(>|z|)     S  2.5 % 97.5 %
#>    -0.242    0.00855 -28.4   <0.001 585.7 -0.259 -0.226
#> 
#> Term: ins_unins
#> Type: positive
#> Comparison: 1 - 0
avg_comparisons(fit, variables = "ins_unins", type = "amount")
#> 
#>  Estimate Std. Error     z Pr(>|z|)     S 2.5 % 97.5 %
#>     -2603        136 -19.1   <0.001 267.9 -2870  -2336
#> 
#> Term: ins_unins
#> Type: amount
#> Comparison: 1 - 0

Being uninsured lowers the probability of any expenditures by 24 percentage points, and the expected expenditures of someone who has any by about $2,600. Both are averaged over the whole sample, so the two effects are for the same people. newdata = subset(exp_tot > 0) averages the amount effect over only the people with any expenditures, the observations the second part was fit to:

avg_comparisons(fit, variables = "ins_unins", type = "amount",
                newdata = subset(exp_tot > 0))
#> 
#>  Estimate Std. Error     z Pr(>|z|)     S 2.5 % 97.5 %
#>     -2833        148 -19.2   <0.001 270.3 -3122  -2544
#> 
#> Term: ins_unins
#> Type: amount
#> Comparison: 1 - 0

Among the people with any expenditures, being uninsured is associated with about $2,830 less in expenditure. This describes the people who spend, but it is averaged over different observations than the first part’s effect, so the two can differ partly because the observations used to calculate the marginal effect differ.

How well the model predicts

The correlation between the outcome and its expected value summarizes how well a two-part model predicts. It depends only on the expected outcome, so it applies with any second part:

p <- predictions(fit)
cor(p$exp_tot, p$estimate)
#> [1] 0.3916091

The correlation is .392.

Other second parts

The second part can also be a Gamma model with a log link (glm(family = Gamma(link = "log"))), a linear model (lm()), or a negative binomial model (MASS::glm.nb()); twopart works the same way with each. With a linear model of the log of the outcome, add retransform = "duan" for Duan’s (1983) smearing estimate or retransform = "normal" for the normal-theory retransformation:

meps$ln_exp <- ifelse(meps$exp_tot > 0, log(meps$exp_tot), NA)
ln_amount <- lm(ln_exp ~ age + female + lninc + pcs12 + mcs12 + ins_unins +
                  anylim, data = meps, subset = exp_tot > 0)
fit_ln <- suest(any, ln_amount, model_names = c("Any", "LnAmount"),
                cluster = "duid", twopart = TRUE, retransform = "duan")
avg_slopes(fit_ln, variables = c("age", "ins_unins"))
#> 
#>       Term Contrast Estimate Std. Error     z Pr(>|z|)     S   2.5 % 97.5 %
#>  age          dY/dX     94.2       3.53  26.7   <0.001 517.9    87.2    101
#>  ins_unins    1 - 0  -3110.5      79.90 -38.9   <0.001   Inf -3267.1  -2954
#> 
#> Type: response

Comparing two-part models

This example compares two second parts: a Gamma model with a log link, and Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood. Both share the first part, a logit of whether a person had any expenditures. twopart names the two pairs, each a first part and its second part; Any is in both:

any <- glm(I(exp_tot > 0) ~ age + female + lninc + ins_unins,
           family = binomial, data = meps)
gamma <- glm(exp_tot ~ age + female + lninc + ins_unins,
             family = Gamma(link = "log"), data = meps, subset = exp_tot > 0)
poisson <- glm(exp_tot ~ age + female + lninc + ins_unins,
               family = quasipoisson, data = meps, subset = exp_tot > 0)

fit2 <- suest(any, gamma, poisson, model_names = c("Any", "Gamma", "Poisson"),
              twopart = c("Any", "Gamma", "Any", "Poisson"))
effects2 <- avg_comparisons(fit2, variables = c("ins_unins", "age"))
effects2
#> 
#>       Term       Group Contrast Estimate Std. Error     z Pr(>|z|)     S   2.5 % 97.5 %
#>  age       Any+Gamma      +1         108       5.07  21.4   <0.001 335.1    98.5    118
#>  age       Any+Poisson    +1         100       4.47  22.4   <0.001 366.7    91.4    109
#>  ins_unins Any+Gamma      1 - 0    -2843     115.71 -24.6   <0.001 440.4 -3069.7  -2616
#>  ins_unins Any+Poisson    1 - 0    -2846     115.11 -24.7   <0.001 446.0 -3072.0  -2621
#> 
#> Type: response
hypotheses(effects2, hypothesis = difference ~ pairwise | term)
#> 
#>       Term                              Hypothesis Estimate Std. Error       z Pr(>|z|)    S 2.5 %
#>  age       (Any+Poisson +1) - (Any+Gamma +1)          -8.34       2.11 -3.9616   <0.001 13.7 -12.5
#>  ins_unins (Any+Poisson 1 - 0) - (Any+Gamma 1 - 0)    -3.52      36.81 -0.0956    0.924  0.1 -75.7
#>  97.5 %
#>   -4.21
#>   68.63

The two models give nearly the same effect of being uninsured: expected expenditures about $2,840 lower. The difference between them, about $4, is not significant. The effect of a year of age is about $108 with the Gamma second part and $100 with the Poisson one, and that difference, about $8, is significant.

A two-part model can also be compared with a single model for the outcome. Models not named in twopart keep their own prediction – here, a Poisson model fit to everyone, zeros included:

one_part <- glm(exp_tot ~ age + female + lninc + ins_unins,
                family = quasipoisson, data = meps)

fit3 <- suest(any, poisson, one_part, model_names = c("Any", "Poisson", "OnePart"),
              twopart = c("Any", "Poisson"))
effects3 <- avg_comparisons(fit3, variables = c("ins_unins", "age"))
effects3
#> 
#>       Term       Group Contrast Estimate Std. Error     z Pr(>|z|)     S   2.5 % 97.5 %
#>  age       Any+Poisson    +1         100       4.47  22.4   <0.001 366.7    91.4    109
#>  age       OnePart        +1         101       4.60  22.0   <0.001 355.3    92.4    110
#>  ins_unins Any+Poisson    1 - 0    -2846     115.11 -24.7   <0.001 446.0 -3072.0  -2621
#>  ins_unins OnePart        1 - 0    -3028     109.03 -27.8   <0.001 561.6 -3241.9  -2815
#> 
#> Type: response
hypotheses(effects3, hypothesis = difference ~ pairwise | term)
#> 
#>       Term                            Hypothesis Estimate Std. Error      z Pr(>|z|)     S    2.5 %
#>  age       (OnePart +1) - (Any+Poisson +1)           1.29      0.305   4.22   <0.001  15.3    0.691
#>  ins_unins (OnePart 1 - 0) - (Any+Poisson 1 - 0)  -181.79     13.693 -13.28   <0.001 131.2 -208.626
#>   97.5 %
#>     1.89
#>  -154.95

The one-part model gives a larger effect of being uninsured, about $3,030, or about $180 more than the two-part model, and the difference is significant. The effects of age are close, about $100 and $101, though the difference of about $1 is significant.

References

Belotti, F., Deb, P., Manning, W. G., & Norton, E. C. (2015). twopm: Two-part models. Stata Journal, 15(1), 3-20. https://doi.org/10.1177/1536867X1501500102

Duan, N. (1983). Smearing estimate: A nonparametric retransformation method. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 78(383), 605-610. https://doi.org/10.2307/2288126

Santos Silva, J. M. C., & Tenreyro, S. (2006). The log of gravity. Review of Economics and Statistics, 88(4), 641-658. https://doi.org/10.1162/rest.88.4.641
